# zumir

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zumir/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zumir/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedrobtz/zumir/gh-pages/badges/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zumir/actions/workflows/coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

## Overview

A loop over a numeric vector is often the slow part of an R program. The
usual fix is to rewrite it in C or C++, and that needs a toolchain: Rtools
on Windows, the Xcode command-line tools on macOS, `gcc` elsewhere.
Locked-down laptops, Shiny servers and slim containers often have none.

zumir brings [MIR](https://github.com/vnmakarov/mir), Vladimir Makarov's
small just-in-time compiler, to R. It is vendored, so a numeric R function
or a short C function becomes native code from R itself, with nothing else
installed.

* **No toolchain.** `mir_compile()` compiles an R function, and
  `cfunction()` a C function, in memory, in milliseconds.
* **R's answers, or an error.** A function compiled by `mir_compile()`
  returns what R returns, every number bit for bit. Where matching R would
  be costly, it refuses, and names the construct.
* **The same C everywhere.** `cfunction()` reads no system header and
  links only the C maths library and a few memory and string functions, so
  a source behaves the same on every machine.
* **MIR never ends your session.** A compile error, a bad module, or MIR
  running out of memory becomes an R condition you can catch.
* **A compiler for packages too.** Packages that generate code link to
  zumir's versioned C interface (`LinkingTo: zumir`) and get native
  function pointers back.

## Installation

zumir is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub
with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zumir")
```

Installing it from source needs a C compiler once; using it never does.

## Usage

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zumir)
```

Here is a cumulative sum written as an R loop. `mir_compile()` turns it
into native code with the same arguments.

```{r}
csum_r <- function(x) {
  y <- numeric(length(x))
  acc <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    acc <- acc + x[i]
    y[i] <- acc
  }
  y
}
csum <- mir_compile(csum_r)
csum(c(1, 2, 3, 4))
```

It answers as R does, missing values included.

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
csum(x)
identical(csum(x), csum_r(x))
```

What it cannot match it refuses when it compiles, never by giving another
answer. Here R would return a character vector.

```{r, error = TRUE}
mir_compile(function(x) paste(x))
```

When an R loop is not enough, `cfunction()` compiles one C function. An
argument named in `out` is allocated for the call and returned, and `n`
receives the inputs' length.

```{r}
dot <- cfunction("
  double dot(int n, const double *x, const double *y) {
    double s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += x[i] * y[i];
    return s;
  }", n = "n")
dot(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(4, 5, 6))
```

On a loop over a million doubles, `mir_compile()`'s code ran about 35
times faster than R's byte-compiled function, and within 1.3 times of
`cfunction()`'s. If generated code fails the check zumir runs when it
loads, both fall back to MIR's interpreter, which gives the same answers
more slowly. Where MIR has no code generator for the processor, or the
system refuses memory that is both writable and executable, nothing can
be compiled. `zumir_tier()` says which of these holds in this session.

```{r}
zumir_tier()
```

## Learn more

* [Get started](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zumir/articles/zumir.html)
  walks through the three compilers and the tiers.
* [What `mir_compile()`
  accepts](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zumir/articles/mir-compile.html)
  lists the R subset and every case where it errors instead of answering.
* The [reference index](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zumir/reference/)
  documents every function.

## Acknowledgements

zumir is built on [MIR](https://github.com/vnmakarov/mir) by Vladimir
Makarov: its generator, interpreter and `c2mir` C compiler, from a fork
that carries zumir's patches
([pedrobtz/mir](https://github.com/pedrobtz/mir)). `cfunction()` is
checked against MIR's own `c-tests` corpus, and `mir_compile()` against R
itself.
